title: Quantum Computing in Finance: the Intesa Sanpaolo Experience
abstract_summary: This paper surveys Intesa Sanpaolo's establishment and activities of a Quantum Competence Center (QCC) to explore quantum computing applications in finance. It describes the QCC's objectives, collaborations with academia and vendors, workforce development, proof-of-concept projects (e.g., credit risk and fraud detection), and discusses challenges and future integration of quantum technologies into bank operations.
methodology_description: This paper is a descriptive account of the creation and activities of Intesa Sanpaolo's Quantum Competence Center (QCC). The methodological approach was organizational and exploratory rather than experimental: a bottom-up initiative formed a small multidisciplinary team (software engineers and data scientists) to (1) engage industry vendors (D‑Wave and IBM) and academic partners (Politecnico di Milano, Politecnico di Torino, LINKS Foundation) to gain access to multiple quantum paradigms, (2) identify high-impact financial use cases (credit scoring, fraud detection, credit risk analysis, portfolio optimization, derivative pricing, NLP), (3) develop proofs-of-concept and jointly authored research (including a variant of a quantum credit risk analysis algorithm) using a mix of classical simulation and partner QPUs, (4) build workforce capability via training, master programs, hackathon mentoring and student team support, and (5) publish results and coordinate PoCs to inform future adoption strategy. Activities combined vendor/platform experimentation (quantum annealing and gate-model approaches), academic research collaborations, internal client engagement and capability-building rather than a single controlled experimental protocol.

results_summary: This paper is a descriptive, managerial account of Intesa Sanpaolo’s Quantum Competence Center: its formation, team composition, partnerships (industry and academia), early experiments with both quantum annealers and gate-model devices, applied PoCs in finance (credit risk, fraud detection, portfolio optimization), and scholarly outputs. The authors report organizational learnings (need for combined domain and technical mentorship, strategic value of early vendor relationships) and outline speculative expectations that quantum computing may eventually provide speed or precision advantages in several financial tasks. No empirical demonstrations of quantum advantage for production financial workloads are presented; reported technical results (e.g., a more general quantum credit risk framework) are published separately and noted to increase circuit complexity while improving modeling realism.
quantum_advantage_detail: The paper discusses theoretical/expected advantages of quantum computing for certain finance problems (speed or precision improvements) and describes PoCs and algorithmic variants, but it does not demonstrate empirical, production-level quantum advantage; claims about advantage are forward-looking and conceptual rather than experimentally proven in this work.

What organizational model (team size, skill mix, governance) is optimal to scale a corporate quantum competence center?
How to design training and mentorship programs (e.g., balancing domain and technical mentorship) to efficiently build a quantum-capable workforce?
What are the best practices for integrating quantum technologies with existing IT, data architectures, and risk/compliance frameworks in banking?
